title: Childhood internalizing, externalizing and attention symptoms predict changes in social and nonsocial screen time
authors: Keyes K, Hamilton A, Finsaas M, Kreski N

primary_models.name: Weighted cumulative logistic regression of one-year follow-up social screen time category on baseline CBCL symptom category, adjusted for baseline screen use and demographics
primary_models.location_in_paper: Fig. 1 (p. 2283, forest plot without printed values); numeric ORs for social screen time printed only in Results text p. 2284; full ORs in Supplementary Table 1 (not bundled in the PDF). Interpreted in Discussion p. 2285.
primary_models.design: Longitudinal, two waves. Baseline (wave 1) CBCL symptom category is the IV and social screen time category one year later (wave 2) is the DV, controlling for the baseline level of the same screen time measure (residualized change model). One follow-up observation per child; no repeated measures and no time interactions. Social screen time is the DV in this model. Weekday and weekend social screen time are modelled as separate outcomes, and medium and high categories are each contrasted with 0 h.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 4.0. Baseline Sept 2016-Aug 2018 (N=11,876), one-year follow-up 2017-2019 (10,001 followed up with non-zero weight). Analytic N=9,066 with complete psychiatric symptom, screen time and demographic data (9.3% of the follow-up sample missing; not imputed). Mean age 119.3 months at baseline (range 107-132 months). 48.1% female (n=4,362), 51.9% male (n=4,704). Non-Hispanic White 55.2% (5,002), Non-Hispanic Black 13.8% (1,255), Hispanic/Latino 18.7% (1,693), Non-Hispanic other 12.3% (1,116). Household income <$50k 28.1%, $50-100k 27.9%, >$100k 43.9% (Table 1, p. 2282). Same N reported for all analyses.
primary_models.iv: Parent-report CBCL (112 items, 0-2 scale) T-scores at baseline for total problems, internalizing (subscales: anxious-depressive, withdrawn-depressive, plus DSM depressive), attention, externalizing (subscales: aggressive, rule-breaking). Because of right skew each scale was trichotomized using recommended cut-scores into non-significant (reference), borderline, and clinical (typically borderline 65-69 and clinical 70+; for internalizing, externalizing and total problems borderline 60-63 and clinical 64+), and dummy-coded. Baseline clinical prevalence (Table 1): total problems 6.8%, attention 2.8%, internalizing 9.8%, depressive 3.1%, anxious-depressive 2.9%, withdrawn-depressive 2.4%, externalizing 5.7%, aggressive 2.2%, rule breaking 2.1% (194). Only the contrasts for which a social screen time OR is printed are extracted here: clinical vs non-significant for total problems, internalizing, withdrawn-depressive, externalizing and rule breaking.
primary_models.dv: Social screen time = sum of youth-reported hours texting, using social media, and video chatting (Youth Screen Time Survey; each item on a 7-point scale 0=none, 0.25=<30 min, 0.5=30 min, 1, 2, 3, 4=4+ hours), computed separately for a typical weekday and weekend day. Because of right skew, trichotomized by percentile rank (1-33, 34-66, 67-100) pooled across waves 1 and 2: 0 h (reference), 0.25-0.5 h (medium), 0.75-12 h (high), for both weekday and weekend social. Composite is built exclusively from phone/SM/digital-socializing items, so it qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2. Distribution at baseline: weekday social 0 h 47.8%, 0.25-0.5 h 33.5%, 0.75-12 h 18.7%; weekend social 50.1%/28.8%/21.2%. At follow-up: weekday social 36.8%/31.7%/31.5%; weekend social 37.2%/27.5%/35.3% (Table 1, p. 2282).

covariates.detail: Baseline level of the same screen time outcome (residualized change model)

covariates.name: Race/ethnicity
covariates.detail: Non-Hispanic White (reference), Non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic/Latino, Non-Hispanic Other

primary_models.equation: logit P(SocialST_followup[i] >= k) (or category-k vs 0 h contrast) = a_k + b1*CBCL_borderline[i] + b2*CBCL_clinical[i] + b3..*SocialST_baseline[i] + b4*male + b5*age_months + b6..b8*race/ethnicity + b9..b10*income, weighted by ABCD ACS propensity weight; fitted separately for each CBCL scale and for weekday vs weekend social screen time. Focal estimate exp(b2) for medium and high outcome categories.
primary_models.estimation: Cumulative logistic regression in R with the VGAM package, run separately for each CBCL scale x screen outcome combination. ABCD propensity weight approximating the American Community Survey sociodemographics of 9- and 10-year-olds applied. No random effects for site or family are described. No multiple-comparison correction reported. Alpha not stated; significance here is judged by whether the 95% CI excludes 1. No p-values printed. No sex or race interaction or stratified analyses reported. Separate ORs are reported for the medium and high outcome categories (Fig. 1), which is not what a single proportional-odds cumulative logit returns, so the exact parameterization (non-parallel cumulative logit or category-specific contrasts) is unclear. The very narrow CIs (e.g., 0.74-0.75) suggest the weights may have been treated as frequency weights.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the OR and to each CI bound
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: clinical vs non-significant baseline CBCL category; OR for being in the medium or high (vs 0 h) social screen time category one year later. M2: 'higher' baseline social screen time category vs 0 h; OR for clinical (vs non-significant) CBCL category one year later.
d_transformation.notes: All extracted cells are ORs with 95% CIs from the Results text, so the Chinn conversion can be applied mechanically. Marked partial because (1) most of the paper's social screen time estimates are only plotted in Fig. 1 or in the unbundled Supplementary Tables 1-2, so only 16 of the social cells are numerically extractable; (2) the ORs come from an ordinal/categorical model whose exact parameterization (separate medium and high ORs) is unclear, so the logistic-latent-variable assumption behind Chinn is approximate; (3) both IV and DV are categorical, so the d reflects a group contrast (clinical vs non-significant, or exposure category vs 0 h), not a per-unit slope, and is not comparable to per-SD d's from continuous-IV papers. No SDs needed. Baseline prevalence for categories is in Table 1 p. 2282; follow-up CBCL prevalence is not reported. Very narrow CIs likely reflect weighting and should not be used for precision-weighting without checking.

extraction_flags: The bundled PDF has no supplement. Fig. 1 plots the main results with no printed values, and the full ORs are in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2, which are not in the PDF. Only the 16 social-screen-time ORs printed in the Results text (pp. 2284-2285) were extracted: 12 for M1 (symptoms predicting social screen time) and 4 for M2 (social screen time predicting symptoms). No values were read off the figure. The remaining social cells are listed under excluded_models and should be added from the supplementary tables if those can be obtained. Social screen time is texting + social media + video chat, which qualifies under FT-IC2 Step 2. The 0 / 0.25-0.5 / 0.75-12 h cut-points apply to social time; the nonsocial measure has its own cut-points. Ambiguities: (1) For total problems, the text does not say whether the weekday 1.02 and weekend 1.15 ORs are for the medium or high category. I assigned them to high based on where the points sit in Fig. 1; please verify. (2) In M2 the text says "higher" social screen time without naming medium or high vs 0 h. (3) The paper calls the method cumulative logistic regression in VGAM, yet it reports separate ORs for the medium and high categories. That does not fit a single proportional-odds model, so the parameterization is unclear and the Chinn conversion is only approximate. (4) No p-values are printed; sig is set from whether the 95% CI excludes 1. (5) The CIs are implausibly narrow (e.g., 0.74-0.75), which suggests the propensity weights were treated as frequency weights. Be careful using these CIs for precision weighting. (6) Follow-up CBCL prevalence is not reported, so p0 is null.
